meta.title: String stars, small black holes, and the supersymmetric index
meta.abstractHtml:
We discuss aspects of the black hole-string transition as the angular velocity approaches the supersymmetric index . In this limit, the high-temperature Atick-Witten effective description breaks down. For Heterotic string theory, a new high-temperature description emerges near the index in terms of a Higgsed supergravity with a magnetic field profile. The Hagedorn instability manifests in the theory as Ambjørn–Olesen W boson condensation, due to the background magnetic field. For type II, a tower of winding strings becomes light near the index, which opens up a new dimension in the T-dual picture. In both cases, a string star solution is found, similar to the Horowitz-Polchinski solution, but decouples at the index .
Considering charged solutions, the string star appears to interpolate between charged black holes and the free string phase. At the index, both the charged black hole and the charged string star phases decouple. This suggests a tension between a smooth black hole-string transition and the existence of a stringy BPS two-charge black hole.

children.title: Abstract
children.body:
We discuss aspects of the black hole-string transition as the angular velocity approaches the supersymmetric index . In this limit, the high-temperature Atick-Witten effective description breaks down. For Heterotic string theory, a new high-temperature description emerges near the index in terms of a Higgsed supergravity with a magnetic field profile. The Hagedorn instability manifests in the theory as Ambjørn–Olesen W boson condensation, due to the background magnetic field. For type II, a tower of winding strings becomes light near the index, which opens up a new dimension in the T-dual picture. In both cases, a string star solution is found, similar to the Horowitz-Polchinski solution, but decouples at the index .
Considering charged solutions, the string star appears to interpolate between charged black holes and the free string phase. At the index, both the charged black hole and the charged string star phases decouple. This suggests a tension between a smooth black hole-string transition and the existence of a stringy BPS two-charge black hole.

The high-energy spectrum of quantum gravity is dominated by black holes. In weakly coupled string theories, there is an intermediate high energy limit dominated by highly excited strings with a Hagedorn growth [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. It is an old question [6, 7, 8], whether these two thermodynamic phases are secretly one and the same. Namely, if a high-temperature black hole (say in the last stages of evaporation) transitions to a self-gravitating string state, or a ‘string star’. This is sometimes referred to as the black hole/ string transition. Since the two phases have no reliable overlapping region, attempts to argue for or against them have always been mostly qualitative.

gist.html: Poses the old question: does a string-scale black hole turn into a self-gravitating string, a “string star”?

children.body: This work studies the fate of the black hole/ string transition at the (target space) -BPS supersymmetric index of either Heterotic or type II strings on . This index can be reached continuously from the thermal partition function, by turning on an angular velocity at . For a given set of charges , the exact index is known [9, 10] by a free string theory calculation. One may ask for the contribution of either the black hole or the string star to the index, by following them to the value . Since the index is independent of temperature and string coupling, agreement or disagreement between the two phases and the microscopic answer could shed light on the nature and validity of the string-black hole transition itself.

gist.html: The exact index, reached by an imaginary angular velocity, could test the transition independently of temperature and coupling.

children.title: The index as a twisted partition function
children.body: A supersymmetric theory has a conserved fermion number $(-1)^F$ and supercharges that pair every state of non-zero energy with a partner of opposite statistics. In the trace $\operatorname{Tr}\,e^{-\beta H}(-1)^F$ such pairs cancel, so only states annihilated by some supercharges, the BPS states, contribute, and the result does not change with $\beta$ or with any continuous coupling. For strings on $\mathbb R^d$ the relevant object is a half-BPS index that counts states with given momentum and winding charges; it can be computed at zero string coupling and gives $S_\text{micro}=4\pi\sqrt{|Q_nQ_w|}$. The paper's observation is that this index is also a point in a continuous family: since rotating by $2\pi$ gives $(-1)^F=e^{2\pi iJ}$, inserting $e^{-\beta\Omega J}$ with $\beta\Omega=2\pi i$ into the thermal partition function produces exactly the index, so one can turn the angular velocity on gradually and watch each saddle of the thermal problem move towards $\nu=0$.

Unlike the black hole, it is not clear at all how to deform the string star saddle away from the thermal case. To understand why, let us recall what the string star saddle really is. We denote the radius of the thermal circle. Viewing the canonical partition function as a Euclidean string amplitude, a mode with a single winding along the thermal circle turns tachyonic for , accounting for the Hagedorn growth of string states. Upon reducing on the thermal circle, one obtains the Atick-Witten effective field theory (EFT) [5], which includes all the standard massless spectrum, together with a “thermal scalar”: a complex scalar with mass . The string star saddle, or the Horowitz-Polchinski solution [11, 12], is a normalizable solution for the thermal scalar coupled to Newtonian gravity.1 The Atick-Witten EFT is reliable as long as the thermal scalar mass is light, which happens slightly below the Hagedorn temperature . Perturbatively in , one can employ the Atick-Witten EFT to find slowly rotating string star solutions [16]. But as we turn on , the potential for the thermal scalar becomes string-sized, leading to an unreliable EFT. Thus, it appears hopeless to reliably deform the string star saddle to the index.

gist.html: The Horowitz–Polchinski string star cannot simply be followed to the index: its effective theory fails at order-one rotation.

children.title: The thermal circle and the winding tachyon
children.body: A thermal partition function $\operatorname{Tr}\,e^{-\beta H}$ equals a path integral in imaginary (Euclidean) time, with time periodic of length $\beta=1/T$: the trace glues the final state to the initial one. A thermal system therefore lives on space times a circle. A particle can only move around this circle, but a closed string can also wrap it, and the wrapped string's mass squared is its stretching energy, which grows with the circle, minus a zero-point energy. On a small enough circle, at high enough temperature, the zero-point term wins and the wrapped string becomes tachyonic. A tachyon is a direction in which the Euclidean action is unbounded below, so the partition function diverges: this is the Euclidean face of the Hagedorn growth of string states. Just before that point the wrapped string is a light field, with mass squared proportional to $R-R_H$, and that light field is what the Atick–Witten theory keeps.

Surprisingly, although the Atick-Witten EFT breaks down, we find a novel EFT close to the supersymmetric point . In section 2, we begin with Heterotic string theory. At the index, the thermal circle admits a (periodic) supersymmetric boundary condition for the fermions. At the self-dual radius (in string units), the effective -dimensional theory is half-maximal gauged supergravity. Away from the self-dual point, the theory is higgsed back to the standard KK gauge group. This gauge enhancement is a well-known property of Heterotic string theory [30, 31].2 For temperatures close to the self-dual radius , the EFT is reliable. The winding mode takes place in the EFT as the W boson. Due to supersymmetry, the W boson is stable, which agrees with the absence of a Hagedorn instability due to supersymmetric cancellations. By going slightly away from , the Hagedorn instability is restored, and the theory should have a tachyon. In the EFT, this instability has an elegant explanation. Changing amounts to a magnetic field profile for the unbroken in the direction of the rotation plane. Since the W boson is charged, its mass is affected by the magnetic field. The result is known as the Ambjørn–Olesen phenomenon [32, 33, 34], in which the electroweak W boson condenses if the background magnetic field is high enough compared to the Higgs VEV. In our context, it explains how the winding mode (W boson) turns tachyonic away from the index (magnetic field) at high temperatures (small Higgs VEV).

gist.html: Near the heterotic index a new theory takes over: the winding mode is a W boson, destabilised by magnetism.

children.title: How a twist becomes a magnetic field
children.body: Take flat space with periodic Euclidean time, $x^0\sim x^0+2\pi$, and identify points so that going once around the time circle also rotates the $x^1x^2$ plane by an angle $2\pi u$. Locally nothing changes: the space is flat. Now reduce on the time circle, writing the metric as $e^\sigma(dx^0+a_idx^i)^2$ plus a spatial part. In the angle $ heta= heta'- u x^0$, for which the identification is untwisted, the metric acquires a cross term $ u ho^2\,dx^0d heta$. The Kaluza–Klein vector $a$ therefore has a profile whose field strength is concentrated near the axis $ ho=0$: a magnetic field, together with a circle radius and a dilaton that vary with $ ho$. This is a Euclidean Melvin flux tube. Any state with momentum or winding around the time circle is charged under these vectors and feels the field, which is how the paper's W boson sees the twist.

In section 3, we look for string star solutions close to the index. In terms of the EFT, we work close to the critical magnetic field and look for a bubble of W boson condensation. We call those solutions ‘W stars’. Similar to the Horowitz-Polchinski solution, these solutions include a winding-mode profile as well as the gravitational (and magnetic) forces needed to support it. The solution shares many properties with the Horowitz-Polchinski solution, with a notable difference: the W star decouples as we tune back to the index . As we explain, this property is also shared by rotating black holes in this limit.

gist.html: W stars, bubbles of W condensate, resemble Horowitz–Polchinski but decouple at the index, as rotating black holes do.

children.body: Next, in section 4, we use the method put forward in [12] and consider charged solutions. Slightly away from the index, we find such charged W stars and study their properties. Similar to [12], our solutions appear to interpolate between the charged rotating black hole and the free string phase and approach the correct microscopic index . This is drastically different than the charged black hole saddle, where a naive continuation to the index gives a vanishing index. Exactly at the index, however, both the weakly curved charged black hole and the charged W star are unreliable and decouple from the spectrum. Thus, we argue that a smooth black hole/string transition contradicts the existence of a BPS ‘small black hole’ solution of the type recently suggested in [35, 36].

gist.html: Charged W stars approach the microscopic index, yet they and charged black holes decouple, against a BPS small black hole.

children.body: In section 5 we comment on the type II case. Close to the index, an arbitrary number of winding strings become light at the same time. Thus, the EFT in this case is the T-dual dimensional SUGRA [37]. We argue that string star solutions exist with properties similar to the Heterotic W star. In section 6 we consider Bosonic string theory, and explain a possible issue with the black hole/string transition when turning on large imaginary . We close with conclusions and future directions.

gist.html: For type II the EFT is a T-dual supergravity in one more dimension; bosonic strings raise a puzzle.
Followed to the supersymmetric index, black holes and string stars both decouple, against a proposed BPS small black hole.

brief.html: Black holes and highly excited strings have never been compared where both are trustworthy; the index offers a place, because it cannot change along the way. The obstacle is that the usual description of the string star fails once the rotation is of order one. For heterotic strings a gauge theory with a W boson replaces it, and its condensates, like rotating black holes, disappear at the index. Charged saddles and type II strings end the same way, so a smooth transition conflicts with a proposed BPS small black hole.

children.title: Gauge enhancement at the self-dual radius
children.body: T-duality maps a closed string on a circle of radius $R$ to one on a circle of radius $1/R$ (string units), exchanging its momentum $n$ and winding $w$; $R=1$ is the fixed point, the self-dual radius. The string's left- and right-moving momenta are $p_{L,R}\propto n/R\pm wR$, and each side contributes separately to its mass. At a generic radius only $n=w=0$ states are massless, and the circle supplies two abelian gauge fields, the Kaluza–Klein vector and the $B$-field vector, or in a chiral basis $U(1)_L\times U(1)_R$. At the self-dual radius the states with $n=w=\pm1$ have $p_R=0$, while their $p_L$ exactly cancels the zero-point energy of the heterotic string's bosonic side. They become two extra massless vectors of charge $\pm1$ under $U(1)_L$, and the gauge group is enhanced to $SU(2)_L$: the textbook example of stringy gauge enhancement. The radius is then a flat direction of an adjoint scalar, and moving along it Higgses $SU(2)_L$ back to $U(1)_L$. That is why, near the index, the thermal winding string can be a gauge boson.

children.title: Landau levels and the Zeeman shift
children.body: A charged particle moving in a plane with a constant magnetic field $B$ has quantised circular orbits. For a relativistic particle of mass $m$ and charge $q$ the energies are $E^2=m^2+qB(2k+1)$, with $k=0,1,2,\dots$: the Landau levels. Each level is hugely degenerate, with one state per flux quantum, and the lowest is a Gaussian of width $1/\sqrt{qB}$. A particle with spin adds a Zeeman term: the spin component $s$ along the field shifts the energy squared by $2qBs$. For a scalar the lowest level, $m^2+qB$, is always positive. For a spin-1 boson with $s=-1$ it is $m^2-qB$, which turns negative above a critical field: the Ambjørn–Olesen instability. The Melvin field of the paper is not uniform, and that lifts the degeneracy, leaving one lowest state to condense.

children.title: Saddles, their weight, and decoupling
children.body: In the Euclidean path integral of gravity, a partition function is approximated by its classical solutions with the right boundary conditions, the saddles. Each contributes roughly $e^{-I}$, with $I$ its on-shell action, so the saddle of least action dominates; free energy, entropy and energy follow from derivatives of $I$ with respect to $\beta$. A Euclidean black hole is such a saddle, and so is a string star. Each is trustworthy only where its own approximation holds: weak curvature for the black hole, a light winding mode for the string star. When a parameter is tuned so that a saddle's trustworthy regime runs off to infinite size or action, the saddle stops contributing: its weight goes to zero, or it can no longer be trusted anywhere. The paper calls this decoupling, and asks which saddles survive the approach to the index.

At the index, the background is supersymmetric, the Lagrangian is entirely positive, and admits no normalizable saddles.13 Thus, at there are no “W stars” saddles. This is a striking difference with the Atick-Witten EFT. The application of this statement for the correspondence with black holes will be discussed below. For now, the lesson is that in order to find such saddles we must turn on , and shouldn’t treat it as a perturbative parameter. Such a saddle can be thought of as a meta-stable bubble of the W condensation phase. The existence of a high-temperature W boson tachyon for , established in the previous section, is a positive signal that such a bubble solution could be formed.

gist.html: At the index the action is positive, so no W stars exist; $\nu>0$ must be kept finite.

To describe any normalizable string theory saddle of thermal winding strings, we will use the term “string stars” collectively. Thus, both the Horowitz-Polchinski solution and W stars are types of string stars, but not the other way around.

children.title: Why a black hole might become a string
children.body: As a black hole evaporates its temperature rises and its horizon shrinks, until the horizon reaches the string length $l_s$. There the curvature is stringy and general relativity can no longer be trusted. Susskind, and later Horowitz and Polchinski, noticed that at this point the entropy of the black hole and the entropy of a single highly excited string of the same mass agree, up to factors of order one. This “correspondence principle” suggests that the black hole might not end abruptly but become a long string, perhaps one bound by its own gravity. The argument is only an estimate: neither description is reliable exactly at the matching point, so it cannot say whether the change is smooth. The paper makes the same kind of rough comparison near the index, between the W star and rotating black holes.

brief.html: Bosonic strings have no index, and their partition function repeats when the rotation angle $\omega$ grows by $2\pi$. The string star, built on a unique winding ground state, repeats smoothly. Black holes repeat only after summing over branches, which leaves a kink in the free energy halfway. If black hole and string star are continuously connected, stringy effects must smooth the kink at intermediate temperatures; the same issue appears in AdS$_3$.

children.body: We considered aspects of the black hole/string transition close to the supersymmetric index, by turning on an imaginary angular velocity , with . In contrast to the thermal case, the analysis depends heavily on the string theory in question.

For Heterotic strings, we found that instead of the Atick-Witten theory, the effective description is a Higgsed SUGRA, in which the winding mode is the W boson. The Hagedorn instability is manifest (for ) via a version of the Ambjørn–Olesen phenomenon. The string star in this regime is a bubble of W boson condensate, with properties similar to the Horowitz-Polchinski solution. In the limit, the string star decouples from the spectrum, just like the weakly-curved black hole. For type II string theory, an arbitrary number of winding strings are light together for , leading to a new T-dual dimension. The effective -dimensional theory admits a somewhat complicated tachyonic mode for [37]. Nonetheless, a string star solution arguably exists in an appropriate low-energy limit, leading to similar results.

String star solutions with NS-NS charges can be found by generalizing the method put forward in [12], for both Heterotic and type II string theories. The same picture suggested in [12] seems to hold for , in which the string star interpolates between the free string and the black hole phase. Following the uncharged case, the charged string star decouples in the limit. This suggests that both the black hole and the string star phases decouple, leaving only a BPS string phase. However, this picture is in tension with the small black hole saddle suggested recently for the index [35, 36].

gist.html: Concludes that black hole and string star both decouple at the index, in tension with the small black hole saddle.

children.body: For Heterotic strings, the transition to the BPS string phase appears to be smooth. Specifically, for large charges, the charged string star entropy approaches the microscopic BPS entropy. For type II, the transition could be smooth, but requires some crossover in the free string phase from a generic highly-excited string and a BPS string. It would be interesting to find a possible connection to the worldsheet index arguments of [12]. We leave these questions for future work.

gist.html: The heterotic route to BPS strings looks smooth; type II needs a crossover in the free-string phase.

children.body: Using the new effective description for the winding mode near the index, several extensions of this work come to mind. First, we tuned the winding mass to satisfy for convenience, which allows us to consider only the ground state. It would be interesting to study the full solution at intermediate values of the temperatures . Similarly, the Wilson coefficients of the -dimensional theory can in principle be found for any through a worldsheet computation. This could help to gather evidence that the self-force of the winding mode remains attractive and supports the picture we suggested. Thirdly, one can consider several angular velocities at the same time, which will lead in the limit to an even-lower-dimensional theory. For example in we can turn on , which would result in a zero-dimensional theory for . It could be interesting to check that the effective force in this case is also attractive, and to study properties of the W star. It could also be interesting to turn on thermal Wilson lines for the Heterotic gauge fields and study how the solution changes as a result, especially close to new gauge-enhancement points.

gist.html: Suggests extensions: the full solution at $m^2\sim\nu$, worldsheet couplings, several angular velocities, Wilson lines.

children.body: Finally, for Bosonic string theory, we spelled out an important qualitative difference between the black hole and the string star phases. Namely, the black hole has a first-order phase transition at , while the string star has none. Both type II and Heterotic avoid this issue: since both are Fermionic theories, , the phase transition could occur at , not , and second, both the black hole and, due to supersymmetry, the string star decouple at . A different version of this issue arises for fermionic but non-supersymmetric string theories. While the black hole free energy still diverges at , we no longer expect the string star to diverge (the partition function still admits a Hagedorn growth).

gist.html: Supersymmetric theories escape the bosonic kink: with period $4\pi$ it would sit at $\omega=2\pi$, where both phases decouple.
Both saddles decouple at the index, in tension with small black holes; the regime $m^2\sim\nu$ and worldsheet couplings remain open.

brief.html: Both the black hole and the string star decouple at the index, leaving BPS strings. This is in tension with the small black hole saddle recently proposed for the index. The heterotic route to BPS strings looks smooth; type II needs a crossover among free strings. The main gaps are the regime where the condensate is not much lighter than the Landau spacing, and a worldsheet derivation of the couplings.

• Context Do string-scale black holes become self-gravitating “string stars”? The exact supersymmetric index $\beta\Omega=2\pi i$ could tell.
  • Result
    • Near the heterotic index a Higgsed $SU(2)_L\times U(1)_R$ supergravity replaces Atick–Witten; the Hagedorn instability is its winding W boson's Ambjørn–Olesen condensation in a magnetic field.

  • Why it matters This suggests tension between a smooth black hole/string transition and a proposed BPS small black hole.

brief.html:
In weakly coupled string theory, energies $1\ll l_sE\ll g_s^{-2}$ belong not to black holes but to highly excited strings with Hagedorn growth. Whether a black hole heated to the string scale becomes such a self-gravitating string, a “string star”, is an old question, hard to settle because the two descriptions are never reliable together. The paper follows both to the half-BPS supersymmetric index, which an imaginary angular velocity $ eta\Omega=2\pi i$ reaches from the thermal ensemble. The index is exact and independent of temperature and coupling, so each phase can be compared with it. Weakly curved black holes and string stars, neutral or charged, all decouple there: their reliable regimes run off to infinite size or temperature. So if the phases are connected, only BPS strings remain, against a recently proposed BPS small black hole.

The usual string star's effective theory fails at rotations of order one, because the twist opens string-scale gaps. Near the heterotic index the lightest winding state is instead a vector, massless at the self-dual radius: the W boson of an enhanced $SU(2)_L imes U(1)_R$, Higgsed by the circle's radius $R$. The paper writes this supergravity to all orders in the fields at two derivatives. Off the index the twist $ u$ acts as a magnetic field, which quantises the W's motion in the rotation plane into Landau levels spaced by order $ u$. Through its spin one W mode drops below them, to $m^2=(R-1/R)^2-2 u/R^2$, so it is tachyonic below $R_H( u)=1+\sqrt{ u/2}+\dots$ This Ambjørn–Olesen instability of electroweak W bosons is here the string's Hagedorn instability.

Exactly at the index the effective action is positive, so no localised condensate exists. Slightly away, gravity and magnetic forces bind the W condensate into a “W star” in three to five spatial dimensions. Its $S_ u$ (the entropy at $ u=1$, the exponent of the index at $ u=0$) obeys $S_ u=2\pi l_sE$: Hagedorn growth beside an index that has no Hagedorn temperature. It scales like the Horowitz–Polchinski string star up to a logarithm, suggesting one family of string stars. Near the index it does not dissolve but decouples: at fixed temperature its size and action diverge, and at fixed energy its transition to free strings recedes to infinite energy. Rotating black holes decouple too, because their horizons diverge.

Momentum and winding charges make the index non-trivial, with free-string entropy $S_ ext{micro}=4\pi\sqrt{|Q_nQ_w|}$, and a classical duality adds them to any neutral saddle, exactly in $\alpha'$. Charged black holes reach the BPS bound only through string-scale curvature, and the reliable ones recede from it as the index nears. Charged W stars do better: near the heterotic index $S_ u\approx2\pi\sqrt{M^2-Q_L^2}$, which approaches $S_ ext{micro}$ close to the BPS bound. But only within a temperature window, between black-hole and free-string transitions, that closes at the index, so they decouple too. At the free-string transition their size matches a typical BPS string's, suggesting a smooth passage to BPS strings.

For type II strings the winding mass vanishes only at zero radius, so near the index a tower of windings is light. T-dual, they are momentum modes in one more dimension, where a similar string star is argued to exist. Its charged entropy carries a factor $\sqrt u$ and seems to vanish at the index. That zero is an artifact of the order of limits: heavy strings at fixed twist are far from BPS, but those lighter than about $1/ u$ are nearly BPS. For bosonic strings the black hole free energy has a kink in the rotation that the string star's lacks, an open tension.

The W star is built only far below the Landau spacing, and for type II its couplings are assumed, not derived. The black hole comparison extrapolates both saddles to the string scale, where their divergences carry different powers of $ u$. Above all, the paper does not show that W stars and black holes are connected; if they are not, a small black hole could still contribute.

defs.html: A localised, self-gravitating condensate of strings wound around the Euclidean time circle, held together by the long-range forces it sources: a candidate for what a black hole becomes near the string scale. In this paper the term covers both the Horowitz–Polchinski solution and the W star.

The conjectured passage of a black hole heated towards the string scale, say in the last stages of its evaporation, into a self-gravitating string state, a string star. The two descriptions are never reliable in the same regime, so arguments for or against it have been mostly qualitative.

at.quote: referred to as the black hole/ string transition

defs.html: The growth of the number of string states with energy $E$ as $e^{2\pi R_HE}$ (string units): exponential in the energy itself, not in a power of it. It makes the canonical partition function diverge above the Hagedorn temperature.

The trace $\operatorname{Tr}\,e^{-\beta H}(-1)^F$, in which states paired by supersymmetry cancel, so only BPS states contribute and the result cannot depend on temperature or coupling. Here it is the half-BPS index at fixed charges (strictly, a helicity supertrace), reached from the thermal trace at $\beta\Omega=2\pi i$.

at.quote: supersymmetric index of either Heterotic or type II strings

defs.html: Said of states annihilated by some of the supercharges. They form shorter multiplets, saturate a lower bound on the mass set by the charges, and are what the index counts. For heterotic strings the bound is $M\ge|Q_R|$, saturated when the supersymmetric right-movers are unexcited; half-BPS states preserve half the supercharges.

A classical solution of the Euclidean action with the boundary conditions of the trace, such as a Euclidean black hole or a string star. To leading order each contributes $e^{-I}$ to the partition function, where $I$ is its on-shell action.

Euclidean time, which is periodic with period $\beta=1/T$ in a thermal partition function. The paper uses its radius $R=\beta/2\pi$ in string units ($\alpha'=1$, so the string length is 1): $R\sim1$ is a temperature of order the string scale, and smaller $R$ is hotter.

at.quote: the radius of the thermal circle

defs.html: A string state wrapped around a circle, here the thermal circle; its stretching energy grows with the radius. The paper follows the lowest such state as the twist varies: the thermal scalar near the thermal point, the W boson near the heterotic index.

at.quote: a mode with a single winding along the thermal circle

defs.html: The temperature $1/(2\pi R_H)$ at which the string wound once around the thermal circle becomes massless. On a smaller circle ($R<R_H$, hotter) that state is tachyonic and the thermal partition function diverges. Near the index the paper finds a twist-dependent version, $R_H(\nu)$.

at.quote: accounting for the Hagedorn growth of string states

defs.html: The effective field theory of strings just below the Hagedorn temperature, obtained by reducing on the thermal circle: the massless supergravity fields plus the light thermal scalar. It holds only while the twist stays close to thermal, $|1-\nu|\ll1$.

at.quote: one obtains the Atick-Witten effective field theory

defs.html: The complex scalar field describing a string wound once around the thermal circle, light just below the Hagedorn temperature, with mass squared proportional to $R-R_H$. Near the heterotic index the same winding state is instead a vector, the W boson.

The original string star (Horowitz and Polchinski, 1997): a localised condensate of the thermal scalar bound by the Newtonian gravity it sources, found just below the Hagedorn temperature in $2<d<6$ spatial dimensions. It is trustworthy near the thermal point, not near the index.

The circle radius $R=1$ (string units) that T-duality maps to itself. For heterotic strings, states with one unit of momentum and one of winding become massless there, and the $U(1)_L$ gauge field, a combination of the Kaluza–Klein and $B$-field vectors, is enhanced to $SU(2)_L$.

Said of a supergravity with 16 supercharges, half the maximum of 32. The heterotic string on a circle keeps all 16, giving nine-dimensional $\mathcal N=1$ supergravity; “gauged” means some of its vector fields gauge a non-abelian group, here $SU(2)_L$.

Here, the string wound once around the thermal circle, seen near the heterotic index and the self-dual radius as a massive charged vector of the $SU(2)_L$ gauge theory, the analogue of the electroweak W. At the index its mass squared is $(R-1/R)^2$; “W” also stands for winding.

at.quote: The winding mode takes place in the EFT as the W boson

defs.html: The tachyon of the thermally wound string above the Hagedorn temperature, the Euclidean sign that the thermal partition function diverges. Supersymmetric cancellations remove it at the index; the paper shows how it returns slightly away from the index, as W boson condensation.

at.quote: agrees with the absence of a Hagedorn instability

defs.html: The instability of a charged spin-1 boson in a strong magnetic field: the coupling of its spin to the field lowers its lowest energy squared to $m^2-qB$, so above a critical field it becomes tachyonic and condenses. Found for the electroweak W; here it is the Hagedorn instability.

An angular velocity $\Omega$ continued to imaginary values, so that the weight $e^{-\beta\Omega J}$ in the trace rotates the plane by a real angle as one goes once around Euclidean time. At $\beta\Omega=2\pi i$ this is a full turn, equal to $(-1)^F$, and the thermal trace becomes the supersymmetric index.

The parameter $
u$ of the paper's trace, with $ eta\Omega=2\pi i(1-
u)$: going once around Euclidean time rotates the plane by $2\pi
u$. $
u=1$ is the ordinary thermal ensemble, $
u=0$ the supersymmetric index, and small $
u$ means close to the index. An earlier paper by Seitz and Urbach used $1-
u$ instead.

The vector field that comes from the metric component mixing a compact direction with space, after reducing on that circle: the Kaluza–Klein vector. Here it combines with the vector from the $B$-field into the left and right fields $A$ and $\bar A$, whose magnetic profile encodes the twist.

A spacetime carrying a magnetic flux tube along an axis. Here it arises from flat space by twisting the rotation angle as one goes around the thermal circle: after reduction, the twist is a magnetic field near the axis, with a varying circle radius and dilaton.

at.quote: This is the Euclidean version of the magnetic Melvin background

defs.html: The coupling of a particle's spin to a magnetic field, here the term $F^{ij}W_iW^*_j$ of the W action. It moves the energy squared of the two in-plane W polarisations up or down; the lowered one is what turns tachyonic.

The string star near the heterotic index: a localised, metastable bubble of condensed W bosons held together by gravity and magnetic forces. It exists only slightly away from the index, $\nu>0$, and decouples as $\nu\to0$.

Said of a saddle whose trustworthy regime disappears in a limit: as $\nu\to0$ its size and action grow without bound, so its weight $e^{-I}$ vanishes and it stops contributing. It does not mean the solution dissolves. When the paper says the $SO(32)$ gauge fields decouple, it means only that they play no part in the analysis.

at.quote: the W star decouples as we tune back to the index

defs.html: Black holes with angular momentum: Kerr in four dimensions, Myers–Perry in more. Here they are continued to imaginary spin so that, in Euclidean signature, they carry the real twist $\nu$; as $\nu\to0$ their horizon radius diverges.

The paper works on $\mathbb R^d$, with $d$ spatial dimensions and spacetime dimension $D=d+1$; reducing on the thermal circle leaves a $d$-dimensional Euclidean theory. The W star becomes effectively a $(d-2)$-dimensional problem, the rotation plane being frozen.

Related by T-duality, the equivalence of strings on a circle of radius $R$ and of radius $1/R$ (string units), which exchanges momentum and winding. Near the type II index the circle is tiny, so the T-dual circle is large and the light windings become ordinary momentum modes.

at.quote: the EFT in this case is the T-dual

defs.html: A BPS black hole whose horizon area vanishes in two-derivative supergravity, such as the extremal two-charge black hole, which is singular there. Stringy corrections have been proposed to resolve it and reproduce the microscopic count, recently also as a saddle of the index.

The logarithm of the exact free-string count of BPS states with momentum $Q_n$ and winding $Q_w$ on a circle: $S_\text{micro}=4\pi\sqrt{|Q_nQ_w|}$ at large charges. It does not depend on the coupling, so any saddle contributing at the index should reproduce it.

A transformation in the classical $O(2,2)$ duality symmetry of the theory reduced on two circles, chosen to keep the winding mode's charges fixed. It maps a neutral saddle to one with momentum and winding charges and the same tree-level partition function.

at.quote: we follow the solution generation technique

defs.html: A black hole of heterotic supergravity carrying momentum and winding charge along a compact circle, the gravitational counterpart of a string with those charges. Its extremal, BPS limit has zero horizon area in two-derivative supergravity: a small black hole.

Sen's way of reaching the BPS bound from a non-extremal charged black hole: an infinite boost combined with a seed mass going to zero. The result has the right dependence on the charges, but passes through string-scale curvature, where supergravity cannot be trusted.

at.quote: Sen suggested the following scaled limit

questions.q: Why is the supersymmetric index a good place to test the black hole/string transition?
questions.a: Because it is known exactly and cannot depend on the temperature or the coupling. The thermal partition function connects continuously to the index through the imaginary angular velocity $\beta\Omega=2\pi i$, so each saddle, black hole or string star, can be followed there and compared with the free-string count. Agreement or disagreement could then shed light on the transition itself, whereas in the thermal case the two phases are never reliable together.

questions.q: What do $\nu$, $R$, $d$ and $D$ mean, and which limit is which?
questions.a:
The twist is $ eta\Omega=2\pi i(1-
u)$: $
u=1$ is the thermal ensemble, $
u=0$ the index, and “near the index” means $
u\ll1$. $R= eta/2\pi$ is the thermal circle's radius in string units; $R$ slightly above $R_H$ means slightly below the Hagedorn temperature. $d$ counts spatial dimensions and $D=d+1$ spacetime ones. Strictly the trace vanishes at $
u=0$, and the index is a helicity supertrace; this does not affect the leading exponentials.

questions.q: Why can't the Horowitz–Polchinski solution simply be followed to the index?
questions.a: The twist shifts the oscillator frequencies of the rotation-plane fields, so away from the thermal point the winding spectrum acquires gaps of order $|1-\nu|$ in string units. For a twist of order one there is no light field left to write an effective theory for. Only near $\nu=0$ does the spectrum become dense again, with a different light field.

questions.q: Why is the winding mode a vector at the index and a scalar at the thermal point?
questions.a: At $\nu=0$ the right-moving level of the ground state is $\tilde N=\tfrac12$, a standard NS excitation that can be built with any of the worldsheet fermions $\psi^0,\dots,\psi^8$; together these states form a massive vector. At the thermal point the GSO projection allows $\tilde N=0$ instead, a single state: the scalar. The level flows between the two as $\nu$ varies.

questions.q: What is new about the $SU(2)_L\times U(1)_R$ supergravity action?
questions.a: The gauge enhancement itself is classic, and the theory had been written to cubic order in the fields. The paper fixes it to all orders in the fields at two derivatives, from half-maximal gauged supergravity, and checks that the W mass reproduces the worldsheet exactly. Unlike the Atick–Witten theory, it is not an expansion in small amplitudes.

questions.q: Why is the tachyon an in-plane polarisation of the W?
questions.a:
Transverse polarisations see the magnetic field as a scalar would: gapped Landau levels, all non-negative. The in-plane polarisations carry spin $\pm1$ along the field and get a Zeeman shift of $\pm2
u(1+R^{-2})$. The lowered one's ground level reaches $m^2=(R-1/R)^2-2
u/R^2$, negative below $R_H(
u)$.

questions.q: Why are there no W star solutions exactly at the index?
questions.a: At $\nu=0$ the background is supersymmetric and the Lagrangian is a sum of non-negative terms. Rescaling a putative localised saddle, $\phi(x)\to\phi(\lambda x)$, then lowers its action in more than two dimensions, so no normalisable extremum exists. The W star needs the Zeeman term, that is $\nu>0$, to favour a condensate; it is a metastable bubble, not a perturbation of the index background.

questions.q: Why does the problem become $(d-2)$-dimensional, and where does the logarithm come from?
questions.a: When the condensate is much lighter than the Landau spacing, its profile in the rotation plane is frozen to the ground-state vortex, and only the other $d-2$ directions stay dynamical. Between two vortices gravity still falls off as $1/r^{d-2}$, the law of $d$ dimensions, which in $d-2$ dimensions is marginal. The self-energy then diverges logarithmically at short distance, cut off by the vortex width $\nu^{-1/2}$.

questions.q: What does it mean that the W star “decouples” as $\nu\to0$?
questions.a:
Not that it dissolves. At fixed winding mass it persists, but its size grows as $1/\sqrt
u$, its amplitude squared as $m^2/
u$ and its action as $1/
u$, so its contribution $e^{-I}$ vanishes and it drops out. The rotating black hole does the same: its horizon radius grows as an inverse power of $
u$.

questions.q: In what sense do the black hole and the W star agree near the index?
questions.a:
Neither is trustworthy at the other's temperature, so both are extrapolated to the string scale. In units of $l_s^{D-2}/G_N$, for $D>4$ the black hole has $M,S_
u\sim
u^{4-D}$ and $r_h\sim l_s/
u$, while the W star has $M,S_
u\sim
u^{-1/2}$ and $L\sim l_s/
u^{1/2}$. Both diverge, with different powers: the agreement is that both decouple. At $D=4$ the black hole mass stays finite while $S_
u$ and $r_h$ grow as $
u^{-1/2}$; higher-derivative terms might change this.

questions.q: What is the Sen limit, and why is the small black hole controversial?
questions.a: Boosting a neutral black hole infinitely while its mass goes to zero reaches the BPS bound with the right charge dependence of the entropy. But the limit passes through string-scale curvature, and in supergravity the horizon area vanishes. Some argue that $\alpha'$ corrections give a finite area matching $S_\text{micro}$, others that the solution stays singular; a recent alternative is a transition to a charged string star.

questions.q: Does the charged W star reproduce the microscopic index?
questions.a: Approximately. Near the heterotic index its entropy is $S_\nu\approx2\pi\sqrt{M^2-Q_L^2}$, and when strongly boosted it nears the BPS bound with $S\approx2\pi\sqrt{Q_R^2-Q_L^2}=S_\text{micro}$. But no W star saturates the bound exactly, and its window of trustworthy temperatures closes as $\nu\to0$.

questions.q: What exactly is the tension with BPS small black holes?
questions.a: If the transition is smooth, the charged black hole continues into the charged W star, and both decouple at the index; the W star ends as BPS strings of the expected size. Then nothing black-hole-like contributes at $\nu=0$, contrary to the proposed BPS small black hole saddle. The alternative is that black hole and W star are not connected at all.

questions.q: What does the paper not show?
questions.a: It does not construct the W star when the condensate is comparable to the Landau spacing, nor derive the type II couplings from the worldsheet. The black hole comparison extrapolates both saddles to the string scale and agrees only qualitatively. Above all it does not show that W stars and black holes are connected: the conclusion against small black holes holds only if the transition is smooth.

questions.q: Why is type II so different from heterotic near the index?
questions.a: For type II the winding ground state has $m^2=R^2-2\nu$, the classical stretching energy with no quantum shift, so it is light only at $R\ll1$, and then every winding number up to order $1/\sqrt\nu$ is light at once. No $d$-dimensional theory holds that many fields; the T-dual circle is large, and supergravity in one more dimension takes over.

questions.q: Why does the type II index seem to vanish, and how is that resolved?
questions.a:
The charged entropy carries a factor $\sqrt
u$, because a typical heavy type II string at fixed $
u$ excites both chiralities and is far from BPS. The free-string partition function shows the limits do not commute: strings with $M\ll1/
u$ are nearly BPS. So the free-string phase that the string star turns into plausibly crosses over to the BPS entropy at lower mass.

The bosonic partition function is periodic in $\omega=-i\beta\Omega$ with period $2\pi$, and the string star respects this smoothly. The black hole phase respects it only after summing branches, which leaves a kink, a first-order transition, at $\omega=\pi$. If the two phases connect, the kink must appear at intermediate temperature and be smoothed by tree-level stringy effects, which is unusual.

questions.q: What is the Hagedorn growth of states, and why does it matter here?
questions.a: The number of string states of energy $E$ grows like $e^{2\pi R_HE}$, exponentially in the energy, so the canonical partition function diverges above the Hagedorn temperature. A black hole's entropy grows differently, as $E^{(D-2)/(D-3)}$. Which phase dominates, and whether one turns into the other, is a question about these two laws meeting at the string scale.

questions.q: In short, what is a string star, and how is it unlike a black hole?
questions.a: A string star is a ball of thermally wound strings bound by the gravity, and here also the magnetic force, that they source, described by an effective theory of the light winding mode. It has no horizon, its size is set by the winding mass rather than by $G_NM$, and it exists only in a narrow window of temperatures near the Hagedorn point.
